ds: A tinkerer who trades grounded machinery for lift and drift, gaining a stored charge that powers hover and flight tricks other Artificers can't.
Artificers who create potions and reagents through experimental science.
Artificers who build a magical suit of armor and fight in it.
Artificers who deploy magical cannons.
Artificers who fight alongside a steel defender.
An artificer who weaponises disease and infection, turning biological processes into armaments.
An artificer who etches power into gear rather than building it in, granting temporary magical properties to weapons and armor.
An artificer who powers constructs with captured fragments of spirit rather than raw mechanism.
A barbarian who grows and hardens by spending their own blood, trading hit points for damage resistance and raw size.
A barbarian who rages to destroy, not just to fight, leaving wrecked terrain and prone enemies in their wake.
Barbarians whose rage leaks raw, unpredictable magic.
Barbarians who call on the spirits of their ancestors to shield their allies.
Armored brawlers who fight in spiked armor. (Originally dwarf-only in the book; many tables drop that restriction.)
Barbarians whose rage reveals a bestial form within.
The simplest, most violent barbarian path — rage turned into more damage and more attacks, at the cost of vulnerability once it ends.
Barbarians who draw on the might of giants.
A barbarian whose rage summons a storm aura — this vault leans on the Sea variant.
A barbarian who channels an animal spirit — bear, eagle, or wolf — into their rage.
Barbarians who draw on the cosmic tree whose roots and branches connect the realms. (Player's Handbook (2024))
A barbarian whose rage is religious fervor, empowered by a god and hard to put down.
A barbarian whose rage calls down lightning rather than just muscle, arcing bolts to nearby foes mid-swing.
A bard who performs funeral rites and battlefield dirges, steadying allies while unsettling the dying.
Bards who channel the song that shaped the world.
Bards whose performance is movement: dancers who fight as they perform. (Player's Handbook (2024))
A bard who plays on sleep and dream rather than waking emotion, drowsing enemies and walking into their nightmares.
A bard whose magic repeats and layers rather than striking once, echoing spells onto second targets.
Masters of oratory and persuasion.
Bards who wield fey enchantment — beauty, charm, and command.
A bard who collects secrets and knowledge rather than fighting spirit — versatile magic and social utility over any single trick.
Storytellers who channel spirits through their tales.
Blade-dancing performers who fight as they entertain.
Battle-poets who inspire allies from the front lines.
Bards who trade in fear, secrets, and stolen identities.
A bard who specialises in the music of war — battle hymns, war drums, and the songs that drive armies forward.
Clerics of a god of magic, blending divine and arcane.
A cleric who channels starlight rather than a single god's word, pulling gravity and stepping briefly into an incorporeal astral form.
A cleric who channels fire rather than a single domain of a living god, wreathing melee strikes and allies in flame.
Clerics of smithing gods who craft and armor.

Grave Domain expands the fantasy and gameplay style of the Cleric class.
 This subclass focuses on a unique identity, combat role, and spell progression.
A cleric of a death deity who serves as intermediary between the living and the dead, guiding souls both ways.
Clerics of lore, learning, and secrets.
The purest healing-focused cleric — every restoration spell goes further, and the domain's whole identity is keeping a party standing.
Clerics of dawn, fire, and truth who wield radiance as a weapon.
Clerics of wild gods of beasts and growth.
Clerics of law, discipline, and authority.
Clerics of harmony who bind allies together.
